entries.title: How can a fire change which plants grow in a forest?
entries.answer: Fire may harm trees and animals, but some ecosystems developed with fires from time to time. In some forests, fires remove low plants that compete for sunlight. Heat can open some kinds of tightly closed cones, releasing seeds. Plants may also sprout again from roots that survived below ground. An unusually severe fire can leave very different effects than a mild one, so what grows back depends on the place and the fire.
facts: Scientists compare plants before and after fires to learn how a forest changes.

entries.title: How can a garden feed pollinators from spring to fall?
entries.answer: One kind of flower may give bees food for only part of the year. A garden can grow several kinds of plants, with some that bloom early and others that flower in summer or fall. Local native plants often suit nearby pollinators, though the best choices depend on where the garden is. A small garden can provide a place for insects to stop and feed as they move across a neighborhood.
facts: Bees are not the only visitors. Some butterflies, flies, and beetles can move pollen too.

entries.title: How can a pile of oysters become a reef again?
entries.answer: An oyster can attach to a hard object. If many oysters grow next to and on top of one another, their shells form a rough structure with cracks and ledges. Small animals can hide there. Oysters also filter tiny pieces of food from water as they feed. Where older reefs have disappeared, groups can restore them by providing clean shells or another firm base for young oysters to attach to and grow.
facts: Fish and crabs can find food around a reef made of oysters.

entries.title: How can a street tree cool a sidewalk?
entries.answer: A tree’s leaves block some sunlight before it reaches the ground. A sidewalk under those leaves can stay cooler than a sidewalk in bright sun. Trees can also move water from their roots to their leaves and release it into the air as water vapor. That change uses some heat. A single tree has a small area of shade, but many trees can shade paths and buildings across a neighborhood.
facts: The shadow of a street tree moves during the day as the angle of sunlight changes.

entries.title: How can an animal return to a place where it disappeared?
entries.answer: A species may disappear from one place while still living somewhere else. Reintroduction means bringing some back to a suitable place in its former range. Before releasing animals, teams study threats, food, shelter, and other wildlife already there. A very rare species may need young raised in a protected setting. After release, people check whether the animals survive, find food, and have young. The hope is for a wild group that can continue on its own.
facts: Black-footed ferrets returned to some parts of the American prairie through reintroduction.

entries.title: How can city lights affect birds flying at night?
entries.answer: Some birds travel at night, when the air may be cooler. Bright lights from buildings can draw some flying birds toward lit areas, where they may get confused or fly into windows. The lights people use can change the way a night sky looks, especially when light shines up from the ground. Turning off lights that are not needed during migration can help reduce the problem.
facts: Many birds migrate, but some travel mainly during the day and others mainly at night.

entries.title: How can people count the kinds of life in a park?
entries.answer: During a bioblitz, people search one area for as many kinds of living things as they can find in a short time. One group might watch birds while another looks closely at plants. They record where and when they saw each kind. The list is a useful snapshot, but living things can be missed if they are hidden, active at night, or easier to spot in another season.
facts: A snapshot from one visit can be compared with later visits that use a similar method in the same place.

entries.title: How can plants help protect a shoreline?
entries.answer: On some quiet coasts, people use native marsh plants, sand, or oyster reefs to protect the edge between land and water. This is called a living shoreline. Plant roots help hold soil in place, and shallow plants or reefs can soften the push of small waves. Fish and crabs can still use the shallow edge to hide and find food. Planners choose which materials will work at each site.
facts: Living shorelines are most often used where the coast is sheltered from powerful ocean waves.

entries.title: What does it mean when a species is endangered?
entries.answer: An endangered species is one that is in danger of disappearing. If the last living member is gone, the species is extinct. A species can be in trouble because it has little habitat left, because there are too few young growing up, or because changing conditions make it harder to find food. Scientists look at where a species lives, how many are there, and whether groups are getting smaller. Those clues can help people decide how to protect it.
facts: A kind of animal can disappear from one region and still be alive somewhere else.

entries.title: What happens when a habitat is split into pieces?
entries.answer: Picture a wide forest cut into smaller patches by roads and open fields. An animal that will not cross those spaces may reach only part of the forest it once used. A tree can stay in one place, but its seeds or pollen may have a harder time getting from one patch to another. The new forest edges can also be sunnier or windier than the old forest interior. This splitting into patches is called habitat fragmentation.
facts: Whether two patches feel cut off depends on the living thing. A bird and a ground beetle can cross different gaps.

entries.title: What makes a plant native to a place?
entries.answer: A plant is native to a region when it occurs there naturally rather than arriving because people brought it from somewhere else. A plant native to one part of a country might not be native to another part. Local insects and other animals can depend on some native plants for food or shelter. A plant brought from another place is called introduced. An introduced plant can grow without necessarily becoming invasive.
facts: Some caterpillars can eat leaves from only a few kinds of plants, so the type of plant can matter as much as the number of plants.

entries.title: When does a new plant or animal become invasive?
entries.answer: Some living things reach new places when people carry boats, plants, soil, or other goods between regions. Some newcomers never establish a wild population. Some live in their new place without harming it. One is considered invasive if it spreads outside its native range and causes harm. For example, a fast-growing plant could crowd out other plants that local insects need. A new animal might eat food that another species depends on. Scientists look for actual harm, rather than judging a kind of life just because it came from somewhere else.
facts: A species can cause problems in one area and be useful in its native habitat.

entries.title: Why did wolves return to Yellowstone?
entries.answer: Gray wolves once lived in Yellowstone, but people removed them from the park and few remained nearby. In the 1990s, wildlife workers brought wolves from Canada back to the area. Wolves can hunt animals such as elk, which in turn feed on leaves and other plants. Animals can act differently when a predator returns. Scientists still compare the effects of wolves with other changes, including weather, food, and the actions of people.
facts: Wolves were released into Yellowstone in 1995 and 1996.

entries.title: Why do monarch butterflies fly south in autumn?
entries.answer: Many monarchs from eastern parts of North America head south in autumn. They gather in cool mountain forests in central Mexico, where the winter usually lets them survive without laying many eggs. When weather warms, they fly north and begin laying eggs. Later generations continue the journey. A female monarch looks for milkweed for its young, because monarch caterpillars eat milkweed leaves. Adult butterflies visit flowers for nectar and can use many different kinds.
facts: The fall travelers live longer than many monarchs born in summer.

entries.title: Why do plants along a stream matter?
entries.answer: The strip of plants beside a stream is called a riparian buffer. It can help both the land and the water. Tree roots help hold the bank together, and leafy branches shade the water. Grasses and other plants can slow rainwater flowing downhill, giving some of it time to soak in. Fallen leaves and bits of wood also help make places for small water animals to hide and feed. The plants form a living edge around the stream.
facts: Cold-water fish can depend on shade along streams that would otherwise warm too much in the sun.

entries.title: Why do some buildings have plants on their roofs?
entries.answer: Some roofs are built with a layer for plants to grow in above a waterproof roof. Leaves and the growing layer can catch part of a rain shower. Some of the water leaves again as vapor, and some can flow off more slowly. This can slow runoff. A roof like this can also shade the surface underneath its plants. The roof needs to be designed to hold the weight of plants and wet growing material.
facts: A green roof can slow rainwater but may still let water run off in a long or heavy storm.

entries.title: Why might a bird fly into a window?
entries.answer: A window sometimes acts like a mirror. A bird may see a reflection of tree branches or open sky and try to fly there. A bird can also fail to see clear glass when it looks through to plants on the other side. Patterns placed close together on the outside can help mark the window as a solid surface. A single mark may leave gaps that look like open space.
facts: Glass can reflect a backyard even when a person indoors can see through it.

entries.title: Why would people build a bridge for animals?
entries.answer: A road can cut between places where animals eat, drink, or raise young. A bridge covered with soil and plants can let some animals cross above moving cars. Others use a passage below the pavement. Fences can keep animals from trying to enter the road and guide them to a crossing. People choose locations by finding existing animal travel routes. A crossing can help keep part of a larger habitat connected.
facts: Different animals use different sizes and kinds of passage.
